items.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>
                    A major challenge for the understanding of violence in the past is that our main source of evidence comes from cemeteries, but a significant proportion of the victims of violence are not buried in cemeteries. Iron and Viking Age Scandinavia (c. 500
                    <jats:sc>BCE</jats:sc>
                    –1050
                    <jats:sc>CE</jats:sc>
                    ) is infamous for its emerging warrior ideology and hegemony of violence. Yet, somewhat counter-intuitively, trauma rates have typically been found to be relatively low in cemetery populations. Not everyone was afforded formal burial in cemeteries, however. The BODY-POLITICS project examines a previously neglected mortuary dataset: disarticulated and semi-complete human remains deposited in and around domestic spaces such as longhouses, pits, wells, postholes, and hearths. We report on 12 individuals inscribed with 19 ante- and perimortem traumatic injuries, analysed through osteological, bimolecular and digital imaging methods. The unusual post-mortem history of these individuals, set within a historical context of raiding, enslavement, and ritual violence including potential ‘human sacrifice’, allows us to explore multiple scenarios for inflicted injuries: war-like events (extra-community violence), interpersonal and domestic violence (intra-community violence), and ritual violence. Finally, by integrating trauma patterns, mortuary treatment, and contextual information, we discuss the broader life histories of these individuals and argue that some may have been vulnerable to structural, ‘slow’ violence that compounded over the lifecourse. This study thus contributes to broader discourse on direct and structural violence towards potentially marginalised people, as well as connections between ritualised violence and divergent mortuary pathways.
                  </jats:p>

items.abstract: Neanderthal teeth represent one of the most valuable sources of information for reconstructing the biology, behaviour, and evolution of Homo neanderthalensis.Due to the exceptional preservation of dental tissues, teeth provide insights into growth and development, dietary habits, physiological stress, health status, and patterns of daily activity.The present review summarizes current evidence regarding the morphology, development, wear patterns, and paleobiological significance of Neanderthal dentition.Studies of dental development suggest that Neanderthals may have exhibited slightly accelerated growth and maturation compared with modern humans, although some findings indicate only minor differences.Morphologically, Neanderthal teeth are characterized by large anterior crowns, robust roots, and complex enamel-dentine junctions, reflecting both genetic inheritance and adaptation to heavy mechanical loading.Pronounced dental wear and characteristic scratches on anterior teeth indicate frequent use of the mouth as a "third hand" during tool manufacture and material processing.Isotopic analyses, dental microwear, and dental calculus studies demonstrate that Neanderthal diets were more diverse than previously assumed, combining large-animal hunting with substantial consumption of plant foods.Pathological findings, including enamel hypoplasias, periodontal disease, abscesses, and evidence of possible primitive dental interventions, provide additional information about health and survival under harsh environmental conditions.Modern methods such as micro-computed tomography, virtual histology, and isotope analysis have considerably expanded our understanding of Neanderthal life history and adaptation.Neanderthal teeth constitute a key source for investigating human evolution and the biological relationship between Neanderthals and modern humans.

items.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>This study, alongside prior work on crab‐eating macaques with O'Higgins, investigates regional variation in skull sexual dimorphism across different species of Old World monkeys. Findings reveal consistent patterns: the posterior skull regions (mandibular vertical ramus, chondrocranium and, possibly, the cranial vault) exhibit lower dimorphism, which may be related to developmental constraints such as the early formation of the cranial base. In contrast, the snout (including the horizontal ramus of the mandible and oro‐facial regions of the cranium) shows the most pronounced dimorphism, aligned with functional and ecological demands, such as canine size differences and masticatory adaptations. Regional dimorphism patterns, if demonstrated, may aid taxonomic identification (focusing on less dimorphic regions) or sex discrimination (using snout measurements). However, these are, for now, hypotheses and potential contradictions in primate studies (e.g., great apes) indicate the need for standardized measurements and methods, as well as an expanded taxonomic sampling. Nonetheless, exploring regional anatomical variation in relation to sex, and potentially other factors such as age and taxon, is a promising avenue of research that can contribute to elucidating evolutionary patterns in morphological diversity of living and extinct species.</jats:p>

items.abstract:
<jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Runs of homozygosity (ROHs) are suitable for studying population demographic history. This study analyzed whole‐genome patterns of homozygosity and natural selection in Colombian indigenous populations to identify their role in population structure and demographic history.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Materials and Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Individuals from four indigenous groups (Nasa, Pijao, Wayuu, and Emberá) were genotyped using an array of 758,740 SNPs. ROH distribution across the genome and signatures of selection were characterized and compared with reference populations.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      Colombian Native Americans showed a population structure similar to that of Central and South American indigenous groups, with higher genome‐wide homozygosity (mean = 179.40 Mb, median = 168.77 Mb, SD = 98.08 Mb), and the Emberá group showed the highest mean ROH size (2.46 Mb) and
                      <jats:italic>F</jats:italic>
                      <jats:sub>ROH</jats:sub>
                      (0.092). Admixture was negatively correlated with ROH content and length. We described 16 ROH islands and selection signatures, including
                      <jats:italic>EDAR</jats:italic>
                      ,
                      <jats:italic>F13A1</jats:italic>
                      ,
                      <jats:italic>SASH1</jats:italic>
                      ,
                      <jats:italic>IYD</jats:italic>
                      , and
                      <jats:italic>FADS1</jats:italic>
                      , with the strongest ROH–selection co‐occurrence at 2q24.2. These genomic regions showed larger haplotype blocks and reduced diversity compared with Europeans and Africans.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Frequent ROH islands in Colombian indigenous groups revealed homozygous chromosomal regions enriched for genes previously reported to be associated with cancer and metabolic and cardiovascular conditions. These islands harbor highly differentiated alleles in Native Americans, including signals of natural selection. However, the presence of these genes within ROH regions does not imply a direct association with disease in the populations analyzed here. Rather, these findings provide a foundational genomic resource for future phenotype‐inclusive studies of complex disease architecture in Native American populations.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
authors: Angel Criollo‐Rayo, Catalina Rubio‐Vargas, Carlos Puentes, Daniel Molina‐Campos, Mabel Elena Bohórquez, Angel Carracedo, Ana Estrada‐Flórez, Danna Díaz‐Carmona, Fabian Castro‐Valencia, Luis Carvajal‐Carmona, María Magdalena Echeverry
